Day 43 of 100 · Linux Administration

Users, Groups & sudo

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

Linux identity management separates users, groups and delegated privilege so administrative access does not have to mean sharing root.

Architecture / mental model

login identity → UID/GIDs → filesystem/process permissions → sudo policy → privileged command

How it works

Users receive a UID and primary/supplementary groups. Services also use dedicated identities so compromised processes do not automatically inherit broad access.

`sudo` delegates specific privileged operations according to policy and provides an audit trail better than handing everyone the root password.

Group membership should express an actual access requirement. Powerful groups such as `docker` can effectively grant root-equivalent control even when the username never appears in sudoers.

Hands-on reference

id USER
getent passwd USER
getent group GROUP
sudo -l
sudo visudo -c

Verification

Inspect the user's effective groups and `sudo -l`, then test the exact delegated command. Confirm an unrelated privileged action remains denied.

Field note / gotcha

Adding a user to a privileged group can bypass the careful sudo policy you just wrote. Privilege is the union of all access paths.

Security considerations

Use dedicated service accounts, least-privilege sudo rules and secure group membership review. Edit sudoers through `visudo` or validated drop-ins.

What I learned

Identity design is stronger when privilege is specific, attributable and revocable.
